docTitle: Dark patterns: 5 design tricks shops use (Instagram)

slides.title: This button has a *name*
slides.sub: It's called confirmshaming, and it's one kind of dark pattern. Here are five more I see all the time.

popup.no: No thanks, I hate saving money

slides.title: A design that tricks you into doing something you *didn't mean to*
slides.body: Harry Brignull, a UX designer, came up with the name in 2010. And most of the time, dark patterns are intentional.

slides.title: Easy to join, *hard to leave*
slides.body: Joining takes one click. To cancel, you go through page after page of offers.

slides.title: The price changes at *checkout*
slides.body: The shoes were €40 on the product page. At checkout, a service fee you never saw makes it €52.

slides.title: A free trial that turns into a *paid plan*
slides.body: You often get no clear warning before it starts charging. They literally charged me for a year's subscription.

slides.title: The box was *already ticked*
slides.body: You end up paying for gift wrapping you never asked for. In the EU, a pre-ticked box doesn't count as consent.

slides.title: The countdown starts again when you *refresh*
slides.body: A deadline that isn't real is there to make you buy faster. EU law already bans it.

slides.title: In 2023, the EU checked *399 online shops*
slides.of: had at least one of the dark patterns it looked for
slides.body: 42 of them used fake countdown timers.

slides.title: A trick can win an *A/B test*
slides.body: Teams test which version gets more sign-ups. The test can't see who was tricked into signing up.

slides.title: When a button guilt-trips you for saying no, *click no anyway*
